text: "Half flesh, half brass. I have to look at both, and that's going to cost me some effort."
"My toolbox has run dry. The rest is down to your eyes."
"If that's the case, your earlier inference might need a second look."
"This I know. Give me a minute, and that thin screwdriver."
"Decent workmanship, but someone's tampered with it. Look here, the tool marks are fresh."
"Give me some room, and some light. ...Right, let me see."
"I've seen wounds like this at a field hospital. I can tell you when and how it happened."
"You don't need me for this one. The naked eye will do."
"From here on, you're really on your own."
"Ready? I've kept track of all your Reasoning Chains."
"I seem to remember... it was somewhere around there? Have a look over there."
"That, yes, that one. It didn't used to look like that."
"Sherefox, look here. ...Something's changed. I've only just noticed it myself."
"This... doesn't look like it should be here."
"Does this have anything to do with the case? ...Never mind, we'll hang on to it."
"You've been staring at that wall for half a minute. Walls don't confess."
"Why not try another corner? That one looks more suspicious... though I couldn't tell you why."
"Those two have nothing to do with each other. Not even Sophistry can make that work."
"...He's not buying it. Show him something else."
"No luck. The only way in now is something less than respectable."
"The Inspector won't hand over the post-mortem report this time. It looks like I'll have to do it myself."
"Let me take a look at him first. The dead don't lie, but they don't volunteer anything either."
"It's only a small kitchen. Fridge, plate, floor, one thing at a time. I promise I haven't touched a thing."
"Every clock in the place is ticking. Let's listen to them first, then ask the people."
"The boiler's gone cold; the fog hasn't. We start with the body and work outward. And don't let the Inspector's 'closed tonight' hurry you."
"There's no Inspector to back us up here. We'll have to find our own way in."
"Don't jump to conclusions. Start at the door and take things one at a time."
"That's probably enough. Although... I think we've missed a thing or two."
"I can't shake the feeling there's a lot here we haven't seen."
"We've seen everything there is to see. The rest is up to that head of yours."
"Wait, the thing by your feet. I picked it up for you. We can't leave without this, can we?"
"Clean and sharp. I don't even know what to grumble about in the record."
"We only lost a round. The case isn't over, and neither are we."
"We lost, and not prettily. Let's go home; I'll cook something."
"A win is a win. Though a few bits made my hand shake as I wrote them into the record."
"Sherefox, tomorrow's paper... you might want to skip it."
"He was about to speak, and you jumped in at the same time."
"That's what his mouth said. It's not what his hands were doing."
"He kept reinforcing while we kept waiting."
"That round he was protecting something, not about to speak."
"For that last move, that wasn't the card you needed."
"He was waiting for your dashed line. I remember his gesture."
"I didn't see anything. I'm just a passing repairman."
"Those two fit together. Yes, that line is sturdy."
"...Are you serious? Those two things are less related than your sleep schedule and mine."
"It holds together, barely. But the moment someone pokes it, it'll snap right here."
"I'm not objecting. I just want it on record that I did warn you, in case this blows up."
"That line... I'll pretend I didn't see it."
"Now. He can't hold you back any longer."
"He's rattled. A rattled man is the easiest to read."
"Don't rush to cut in on him. Steady yourself first."
"Something this battered, can it really be of use? ...Better than nothing, I suppose."
"That scrap of paper won't hold for long, Sherefox."
"We're running short on time. The police... or someone else... could come and clear the scene any moment."
"It's getting dark. Any later and the locals won't let us stay."
"That's it. Come on, Sherefox, any longer and we'll be shown the door."

Scene 1: Newspaper Front Page (Opening)
【The London Lantern · October 1887】Laurel Pastry Shop's Limited "Clockwork Caramel Pudding" Goes on Sale: Queue Winds Twice Around Baker Street

Our correspondent reports: Laurel Pastry Shop on Baker Street yesterday launched its new "Clockwork Caramel Pudding", famed for its caramel topping shaped like a brass clockwork spring. Limited to forty a day, they sold out within an hour of opening. Among the queue were many ladies and gentlemen who had come specially, including one fox-eared girl whose tail was reportedly "never still from start to finish". Also, this paper's classified column carries a notice: "Fox-Eared Detective Agency seeks a flatmate. Cooks preferred; those afraid of fox fur need not apply."
Scene 2: Agency Living Room (Daily Life; The Night Before)
On my second day in Baker Street, I learned three things. First, the landlady's stew is far too salty. Second, my flatmate is a fox. Third, foxes treat pudding as a national treasure.
(Cradling the plate in both hands, tail swishing nonstop) Arthur, look closely. This is the Laurel Pastry Shop's Clockwork Caramel Pudding. Only forty a day, and I queued for an hour.
It looks... very bouncy.
It's not just bouncy, it has dignity. (Plants a little flag in the plate) "Foxes only. Thieves will be bitten." I'm having it with tea tomorrow morning.
Understood. I won't touch it.
(Opens the drawer, glances at the broken pocket watch, then quietly closes it again) ...
What happened to that pocket watch?
Nothing, nothing, just an old thing. I'm off to bed. Good night.

When she said "nothing", her ears drooped. I served as a medic on the battlefield, and I know that when people lie, the body confesses first. That night I decided to do something. It would prove to be the start of a string of small disasters.
Scene 3: Agency Kitchen (Event; Morning)
(Opens the fridge; her ears snap upright) ...Arthur.
(Poking his head out of his room, hair sticking up) M-morning.
My pudding is gone. The plate is here, the flag is here, the pudding is not. This is a kidnapping. This is a case of puddingnapping.
Could it... be a cat?
We don't have a cat.
A stray. London strays are very nimble.
(Narrowing her eyes, tail swaying slowly) Arthur, did you leave your room last night?
N-no. I slept straight through until morning.
Splendid. Then Suspect Number One in this puddingnapping is the only other person in the whole agency besides me.
Are you accusing me?
No, I'm "interrogating" you. I'll apologise afterwards, if you turn out to be innocent.

Clues can hide in every corner of a scene. Move the cursor; anything that glows as you approach is an Investigation Point, and one click investigates it. There are five types: Examine, Evidence, Testimony, Mechanism, and Locked Area.
Evidence Search

What you find becomes an Evidence Card and goes into your Evidence Book. Each card carries five kinds of Tag: Time, Place, Person, Physical, and Scandal. When you reason later, the game uses these Tags to decide whether two pieces of evidence fit together.
Evidence Cards

Talking to people can turn up clues too. A Testimony Card can be used in reasoning just like an Evidence Card, and it always carries a 【Person】 Tag. You can question the same person at most twice per case, so think carefully about what to ask.
Testimony Cards

The pocket watch at the upper left is your Evidence Search clock. From the next chapter on, every new place you investigate costs one Tick, and when the Ticks run out, you must leave the scene. This chapter takes place in your own home, so time is unlimited. Take your time.
Pocket-Watch Ticks
When you feel you've seen enough, press "End Search". Once you do, you can't go back to the scene, and the clues you missed often end up in your opponent's hands.
End Search
This is where you organise your reasoning. Drag Evidence Cards from the drawer on the left onto the board. The board holds up to 15 cards.
Clue Board

For each piece of evidence, write down "what it proves". Choose one of the three Rationales on the right. All three sound plausible, but only one matches the truth. A card with no Rationale can't be linked.
Rationale

Drag from the brass socket on a card's right edge to another card to link the two pieces of evidence. Two cards that share a Tag and both have correct Rationales are joined by a solid line. This is called a Solid Link.
Drawing Links

If two cards share a Tag but one has the wrong Rationale, or they connect only through a tangential Tag, the line becomes dashed. This is called a Sophistry Link. Cards with no Tag in common can't be linked, and the line simply springs back. What dashed lines mean will be explained in a later, bigger case.
Dashed Lines and Bounce-Backs
Cards strung together by links in a straight line form a Reasoning Chain: 2 to 5 cards, no branching. The board holds at most 3 chains. In a Debate, the weapons you present are these chains.
Reasoning Chains

Each round of a Debate, you and your opponent decide on your moves at the same time, then reveal together. You can't see what they chose, but they give off a "Tell": a line, a small gesture, and a lit claim. In this debate Dominance isn't deducted; you win by pointing out Arthur's 2 contradictions within 3 rounds.
Simultaneous Moves

Arthur puffs out his chest and puts his hands on his hips, claiming he slept straight through until morning. He's about to Assert. The eye icon on the right is wide open, which means the Tell is "Clear": he will definitely make the move it shows.
Reading the Tell

When the opponent is about to speak up, choose "Rebut": aim at the lit claim, have evidence ready that can overturn it, and cut in halfway through his sentence. After choosing your evidence, press "Lock In".
When He Speaks, Defend
When a Cut-In lands, you take no damage and the targeted claim is overturned. But Rebut can only catch an Assert: if the opponent is defending, your Rebut whiffs.
Cut-In

Arthur tugs his sleeve down to hide his cuff: he's about to Reinforce his story. When the opponent is defending, that's your moment to strike. Choose "Solid Chain" and present a chain containing only solid lines.
When He Covers Up, Attack

There are two kinds of attack, Solid Chain and Sophistry, and two kinds of defence, Rebut and Observe. What happens when one meets another is all written in the "Matchup Table" on the right, which you can open at any time during a Debate.
Attack and Defence

Arthur is flustered. This is "Shaken". On the round after he's Shaken, strike with evidence that points straight at the truth and you can "Break" him. He's about to speak again: Rebut, aimed at his last claim, presenting the cuff.
Shaken and Break
Arthur records the gestures you've seen and the opponent's habits in the "Opponent Notes". Next time you face the same person, give them a read first.
Opponent Notes
Arthur is now officially your assistant. From the next chapter on, he can appraise medical and mechanical evidence, and will block one trap for you during a Debate.
A New Partner
From this chapter on, investigating a new spot costs pocket-watch Ticks. You'll only get through about seventy per cent of any scene, so it's up to you to decide where your time is best spent.
Limited Ticks

A "?" on a card means that Tag can't be made out yet. Select the card and press "Hand to Arthur", and he'll appraise it with his medical or mechanical knowledge. Appraisals cost no Ticks, but the number per case is limited. Unappraised Tags can't be used for linking.
Appraisal
Some of the evidence you didn't pick up will fall into your opponent's hands, making their story harder to overturn. The screen will only tell you how many pieces you missed, not which ones.
Missed Evidence

A Debate is a contest of whose reasoning is more self-consistent. The steam pressure gauges at the lower left and upper right are each side's "Dominance". Drive your opponent's to zero and you win; if yours hits zero, you lose.
Debate and Dominance

The row of claims along the top belongs to your opponent, and the lit one is the claim he'll push this round. When he Asserts, the damage is a base value plus 4 for every claim on the table; the more claims you've overturned, the less weight his words carry.
The Claim Chain

On a successful Cut-In you take no damage, the claim is overturned, and you bite back for 30 damage. A Rebut needs evidence that can overturn the lit claim; if you have none, the Rebut button is greyed out, and all you can do is Observe to reduce the damage.
Rebut and Cut-In

The opponent was defending this round, so your Rebut had nothing to catch. Their Reinforce succeeded, the claim returned to the table, and a Reinforce that isn't hit also restores some of their Dominance.
Whiff

A chain segment containing only solid lines is presented as a "Solid Chain". Base damage is 14, and each additional Solid Link adds 0.5 to the multiplier. If the evidence you present happens to overturn the target claim, the claim is smashed. Against a Reinforce, damage is halved.
Solid Chain

You struck just as your opponent struck: both sides take a hit, and in a Clash your chain deals only half its damage. When the opponent is about to speak, Rebut is usually better value than rushing in.
Clash
A half-open eye means "Vague": of the two moves listed below, one is real and one is a decoy. First check whether the two options are the same type. If both are attacks, defending is never wrong.
Vague Tells

The option with a star is more likely to be the real one: opponents have habits, such as "tends to Reinforce after a claim is overturned". These habits are called "Behaviour Rules", and Arthur records each one in the Opponent Notes as soon as he sees it. A star only means "likelier", not a guarantee.
Behaviour Rules
When you can't decide, use "Fox-Ear Instinct": a Vague Tell loses its decoy and leaves only the real move. You get just two per debate, so save them for the key rounds.
Fox-Ear Instinct
An overturned claim disappears, but each round the opponent restates their case and adds a claim back. If the added claim comes from evidence you missed, it's marked in the corner.
Smashing Claims
Losing a Debate doesn't end the game, but the next case starts from a worse position. Only the result of the final battle decides the ending directly.
After the Verdict
After each case, the paper prints "the result as the world sees it", which isn't always the truth. Every issue you read goes into your Scrapbook.
The Newspaper

You read their move correctly. Every time you make a favourable response (cutting in when they Assert, quietly Observing when they Reinforce, answering a trap with solid evidence or Observe, or Shaking them with Scandal evidence), a layer of "Unstoppable" stacks up at the lower left, up to three. Each layer raises chain damage and Cut-In counters by ten per cent; at three layers, a Break needs one fewer piece of evidence. But one wrong response breaks your momentum, and you start over. A Solid Chain against a Reinforce still chips them down, but it doesn't count as a correct read; to stack Unstoppable against a Reinforce, use Observe (or Sophistry, once you've learned it).
Unstoppable

The badges at the upper right show how much Inspector Baskerville trusts you: five in all. The higher his trust, the more post-mortem reports, witness lists and scene access he provides; lose a debate, or use underhanded methods, and his trust drops.
Inspector's Trust

The Inspector has already confidently arrested someone. Before the real investigation, correct his misjudgement: when he speaks, use Rebut to present a piece of evidence that overturns him. Warm-ups don't cost Dominance; get it right in one go and he'll give you extra intelligence; get it wrong three times and he loses patience.
Warm-up Debate
Areas with yellow tape need a permit. In cases where the police are involved, the Inspector will let you in if his trust is high enough; if it isn't, you'll have to find another way.
Scene Access

The opponent loosens his cravat and steps forward: this is an "Onslaught". An Onslaught does 1.25 times the damage of an ordinary Assert. But it is also an opening: Cut In on an Onslaught with Rebut and they lose their footing on the spot.
Onslaught

The opponent's pressure gauge starts to leak: they are "Shaken". For the next round, the opponent takes 1.5 times damage from attacks, and a Break can only be played in that one round. Cutting in on an Onslaught, striking a sore spot with Scandal evidence, or presenting a Solid Chain of 4 or more cards can all leave an opponent Shaken.
Shaken

Now is the time to Break. Present a Striker evidence that points to a single fact, or a Solid Chain of 2 or more cards, and you can "Break" the opponent, stripping away seventy per cent of their Dominance outright. When you Break with a Solid Chain, Reinforce can't stop it and traps can't catch you; when you Break with Rebut, it only works if the opponent happens to speak up.
Break

The opponent was defending, so your Rebut-Break whiffed, and the Shaken state ended with it. Next time they're Shaken, if you can't tell whether they'll attack or defend, a Solid Chain is the safer bet.
Missed Window

A Broken opponent won't concede quietly; they will launch one last counterattack. The counterattack type is always Clear, but you must play the right card to stop it. The Endgame lasts only one round: answer wrongly and you take 30 damage, and the Break is voided.
Endgame

A cornered culprit starts flinging blame around wildly. Wait for him to speak, cut in with Rebut, and present a Solid Chain of 2 or more cards with no Weak Points to finish it for good. Don't Observe, and don't use Sophistry again.
Finishing Up: Culprit

The first time the opponent's Dominance drops to half or below, he will always go on the Onslaught, and the Tell will be Clear. Remember this rule: it's a perfect chance to cut in on his Onslaught and leave him Shaken.
Pushed Too Far

The key evidence you reasoned out correctly in the previous case has quietly been filed away, and is now a "Golden Clue". It points to a single fact and has the greatest attack power. A Golden Clue is not used up when you use it.
Golden Clue

You took his Onslaught head-on, and your position is breached. Next round you can't Rebut, only attack or Observe, and Unstoppable resets to zero. When you see the Tell of an Onslaught, cut in on it with Rebut to avoid being breached. You are also breached when a Sophistry is caught in a trap and Cover doesn't block it.
Breached

The opponent has been driven into a corner: that happens when you cut in on them a second time, or when their Dominance falls below thirty per cent. For the next two rounds they hit harder and can't Reinforce, but in their desperation their Tell is one level clearer. This is both a danger and an opportunity.
Cornered
The rival detective, Victor Crowe, has already sealed off part of the scene. You have less time to search than usual; any evidence you miss, he will pick up and use against you in the Debate.
Rival Detective

A dashed line is a "Sophistry Link": the two cards share a Tag, but one of them has an incorrect Rationale, or they connect only through a tangential Tag. Sophistry has a multiplier of 0.8, higher than Solid's 0.5, but every Sophistry Link leaves a Weak Point on the chain.
Sophistry Links

A chain segment containing a dashed line must be presented as "Sophistry". When the opponent Reinforces, Sophistry punches through their defence at full damage, which a Solid Chain can't do. You can also improvise a new dashed link on the spot, but it too leaves a Weak Point.
Sophistry

Victor pushes up his monocle: this is "Set a Trap". Traps catch Sophistry: if you use Sophistry then, your damage is voided, you take a 25-point crit, and that dashed line snaps next round. But traps do nothing against solid evidence: attack with a Solid Chain and you deal full damage, and he can't Reinforce next round.
Set a Trap

If you think he's about to Set a Trap but you have to use Sophistry anyway, press "Cover" before locking in: if the trap catches you this round, Arthur blocks the crit for you, the dashed line stays intact, and your Notoriety doesn't rise. But Cover can be used only once per debate, and it's spent the moment you lock in, even if he doesn't set a trap. It's a prediction.
Cover
You played no card and quietly watched him set the trap, and now everyone can see it. The opponent gains a Fragile claim, and next round they will definitely attack.
Exposing the Trap
An exposed Sophistry hurts more than once. The papers are watching, and so is the Inspector; if your methods look ugly enough, tomorrow's headline won't be kind.
Reputation

A claim marked "From: evidence you missed" in the corner was put together by the opponent from things you didn't pick up. It can be smashed like any other claim, but it's a reminder that there are things at the scene you haven't seen.
Missed Evidence

Victor predicts that you'll repeat your last round's action and plays its counter first: if you just used Sophistry, he Sets a Trap; if you just Rebutted, he Reinforces. Against this kind of opponent, changing your move is the counter.
Mirror

Victor says "I concede" while tossing his glove on the table: that's the motion of his Onslaught. When the words and the gesture disagree, that's a "Disguise": words can lie, gestures can't. Go by the gesture.
Disguised Tells

Victor won't concede so easily; he'll reveal the card up his sleeve, usually the very piece of evidence you missed. Read his gestures, cut in with Rebut when he strikes, and present 2 or more pieces of solid evidence that overturn his hole card to finish it. Later rival detectives will play dirtier.
Finishing Up: Rival Detective

Beware: the rival detective can Break you right back. If the chain you present contains 3 or more Sophistry links, Cover has already been spent, and you are caught by his trap, you will be "Reverse Broken". The status bar at the lower right will flash red to warn you first.
Reverse Break
This opponent isn't a culprit but a "Protector" who wants to shield someone. He mostly Reinforces his story and shifts the focus, so hard evidence has trouble hitting him head-on.
Protector

When you're unsure how to strike, you can "Observe": play no card this round and let him keep talking. If he speaks up, you take only half the damage and the next Tell becomes Clear; if he Reinforces, you force out a claim he let slip.
Observe
The more he says, the easier it is to let something slip. When he Reinforced, you spotted the flaw, so he gains a "Fragile" claim: any attack that hits it will smash it and deal 10 extra damage.
Slip of the Tongue

His Reinforce wasn't hit, so his Dominance recovered by ten per cent. Against opponents who love to Reinforce, rather than just defending, punch through with Sophistry as they Reinforce, or Observe first to force a slip.
Reinforce Recovery
Evidence with a lipstick-mark Tag is Scandal evidence. Present it in a Solid Chain and hit a claim tied to a person, and the opponent becomes Shaken, no matter how much Dominance he has left.
Scandal Evidence

From this chapter on, opponents hold their nerve better: a Solid Chain of 4 or more cards can only leave them Shaken once their Dominance drops below sixty per cent. Scandal evidence, Golden Clues and cutting in on an Onslaught are exempt from this limit.
The Breaking Line

From mid-game on, a Broken opponent switches to a second story, for example from "I didn't do it" to "I did it to protect someone". In the Endgame, aim at the new, purple-framed story. From mid-game on, a wrong answer in the Endgame costs you 60 damage.
A Second Story

Once exposed, the Protector plays the sympathy card: "Exposing the truth will only ruin everything. Can you bear that?" That is a kind of Reinforce, so strike back. But ordinary physical evidence won't move him. Present a Solid Chain with Motive evidence bearing a heart lock, to prove that hiding the truth will bring a greater disaster.
Finishing Up: Protector

This item can't be taken into a Debate, but it remembers a relationship. In some conversations later, it will open up a new option. Story Evidence is kept in the Evidence Book under "Private Collection".
Story Evidence

It's a long way from London, with no Inspector to open doors and no post-mortem reports. Bodies and machinery must be handed to Arthur to appraise; where you can't get in, you'll have to talk your way in.
No Police Support

Guards won't let you through just because you're a detective. Choose a piece of evidence from your Evidence Book that could persuade him, and present it. Choose right and you get in; choose wrong and a Tick is wasted. You can try the same person at most three times.
Negotiation
Areas with red tape can only be entered by sneaking. Sneaking costs two Ticks, and some places can't be sneaked into no matter what.
Sneaking In
In chapters away from London, there is no Inspector to correct, and so no Warm-up Debate. The more access you win during the Evidence Search, the more cards you'll hold in the Debate.
No Warm-up

From here on, the conditions for a Break are stricter: when the opponent is Shaken, present a chain of 2 to 3 cards with no Weak Points; or first use Observe to force out a Fragile claim, then hit it with 2 or more pieces of solid evidence. A Break strips seventy-five per cent of the opponent's Dominance.
Mid-Game Break

From here on, opponents mostly give only Vague Tells. First check whether the two candidates are the same type; then look for a star, and think about what happened last round: did he just lose a claim? Did you just use Sophistry? His habits are all in the Opponent Notes.
Hard-to-Read Opponents
The opponent has made the same move two rounds in a row. On the third round, he will definitely change his move: you can strike that move off the candidate list.
Third Time, He Changes

When the two candidates are one attack and one defence with no star to go on, look for the move that doesn't lose badly against either. If he might Reinforce or Assert, Observe: if he speaks up, you take half damage and see his next move; if he Reinforces, you force out a Fragile claim. If he might Set a Trap or Assert, a Solid Chain doesn't fear traps.
Cover Both Sides

This Debate comes in two parts. In the first, your opponent is the Countess (a Protector); once you've beaten her, Victor Crowe takes over, with a Rival Detective's style. Your Dominance carries over to the second part and is not restored; Arthur's Cover is available once per part, but Fox-Ear Instinct is shared across the whole debate.
Two Opponents
A claim marked "?" is backed by family evidence you can't get hold of. It can't be targeted yet. Observe can force the opponent to say it out loud; once said, it becomes an ordinary claim.
Offstage Evidence

Victor has taken over. The Opponent Notes have turned to his page: the gestures you learned in Chapter 4 are all still there. He will Disguise his Tells; when you see a Clear Tell without the "Basis" brass tag, watch his hands first.
A Change of Opponent

Victor admits the reasoning you just smashed was only bait, then reveals his real hole card. This move comes with a Disguised Tell: read his gestures, cut in with Rebut as he strikes, and present an "Outside Fact" (that is, a Golden Clue) or evidence made specifically to overturn that hole card. If it lands, it's a "Double Break", and you win outright.
Turning the Tables

Your Reasoning Chains have all been severed and only the last sliver of Dominance remains. But in order to Break you, the opponent has played the most deeply hidden evidence he had, and now it's on your Clue Board too. You get one chance to redraw your links: assemble a chain that meets this chapter's Break conditions using it, and you can land a "Counter Break".
Last-Ditch Rebuild
You've now learned every debating technique. The opponents to come will use them all, mixed together.
Graduation

On the left is the city as you remember it; on the right, as it is now. Find the five things that have changed. A wrong click costs nothing, but after a few wrong clicks, Arthur will start giving you hints.
A Familiar, Unfamiliar City

Evidence with a broken card frame stands in for a clue you didn't get. It can help you survive this fight, but any link you draw with it is always a dashed line, and it can't count as an Outside Fact.
Damaged Evidence

This opponent changes through three styles as their Dominance falls: first a Culprit, then a Protector, finally a Sophist. The opponent type icon changes with them, and the Opponent Notes turn to the matching page. You can only Break them in their final style.
Three Faces

This is a public debate, and the crowd is listening. When the opponent is Shaken, a Solid Chain with no Weak Points deals triple damage; chains containing Sophistry stay as they are. But if a Sophistry is caught in a trap in front of the crowd, you lose half your Dominance at a stroke.
The Weathervane of Public Opinion

The final opponents hold their nerve better still: a Solid Chain of 4 or more cards can leave them Shaken only once their Dominance falls to half or below. A Break needs a chain of 3 to 4 or more cards, and it must include a Golden Clue. A wrong answer in the late-game Endgame costs you 80 damage.
Late-Game Break

A claim in a black-iron frame is the core of the opponent's story. A Solid Chain can still smash it; but to cut in on it as he speaks, your Rebut must use a Golden Clue. A Rebut with Common Evidence will block the hit and counter, but the claim stays on the table.
Sturdy Claims
At a banquet, even questions need manners. The fan at the upper right is your etiquette: each breach of manners costs one segment, and when all three are gone, the nobles will no longer speak to you.
Social Etiquette

This Debate is split into several stages, with no return to the Clue Board in between, and the opponent's Dominance is not reset. Cover and Fox-Ear Instinct are shared across the whole debate, so use them sparingly.
Multi-Stage Debate

Wolfhart will deliberately show weakness or strength; many of her Tells are Disguised. Her words can't be trusted, but her hands don't lie: rapping her knuckles is Set a Trap, a gentle swirl of the wine glass is Reinforce, a cold smile is Assert; set the glass down and then smile coldly, and it's an Onslaught.
Retreat to Advance
You've seen through her. For her, the moment her words and gestures disagree is the moment she shows a weakness. Fox-Ear Instinct can also see through a disguise directly, but you only have two.
Seen Through

Ordinary evidence can't leave her Shaken. There are only two ways: cut in on her Onslaught with a Rebut that includes a Golden Clue; or, once she is at half Dominance or below, hit her with a Solid Chain of 4 or more cards that includes a Golden Clue.
The Wall of Perfect Consistency
The outcome of some rounds has already been written, and nothing you play can change it. The eye in the Tell area is replaced by a locked gear. Survive it, and the next round is yours.
